description_ru: Ноябрь в Венеции: высокая вода, дощатые мостки, пустые кафе и город, который тонет с изяществом. Ироничный путевой очерк о красоте, терпении и резиновых сапогах.
text:
Nobody visits Venice in November on purpose, which is precisely why one should. The summer city is a theme park of itself, thronged with people photographing the people who are photographing them, but in the last weeks of autumn the crowds drain away like water from a bath, the light turns the colour of weak tea, and the place resumes the melancholy dignity of an old actress who has finally been left alone with her mirrors.

I arrived by water, as one is supposed to, on a vaporetto that coughed its way along the Grand Canal at a speed best described as ceremonial. The palazzi slid past in the drizzle, their pink and ochre plaster flaking like the pages of an overread book, and the passengers, mostly Venetians returning from the mainland with shopping bags, discussed the tide with the focus of stockbrokers at the opening bell. That was my first lesson. In Venice, the tide is not weather. It is gossip, politics, and religion rolled into one, and everyone has an opinion.

The phenomenon is called acqua alta, high water, and it arrives when a combination of high spring tides, a low-pressure system and the sirocco wind from the south pushes water up the narrow Adriatic and into the lagoon. The city is built on wooden piles driven into mud, and it has been sinking, by a millimetre or two a year for the best part of a century, while the sea has been rising, so the margin between dry and damp is now thinner than a coat of varnish. Piazza San Marco, the lowest large square in the city, floods first, and with a certain theatrical flourish. A series of sirens, rising and falling in pitch, announces the forecast, and a polite recorded voice tells you, in Italian and English, that the tide will peak at a hundred and ten centimetres, which is rather too many.

I had been warned, and had accordingly bought a pair of yellow rubber boots in a hardware shop on arrival, where the assistant sold them with the air of a doctor prescribing a mild but inevitable tonic. Within an hour, I was glad of them. At dawn the following morning the siren wailed, and I stepped out of my pension into a calle that had, overnight, become a canal. The locals were already on the move, wading with enormous composure, carrying briefcases above their heads, while a man in a waistcoat swept a film of seawater out of his bakery with a broom, as though dismissing an unwelcome guest.

It was, I must admit, extraordinarily beautiful. The square lay under a sheet of water the colour of pewter, in which the basilica hung upside down, its gilded domes and curlicues quivering in a faint breeze. The pigeons, those frequent and unlovely citizens, had retired to the colonnades with an expression of injured dignity. Along the flooded arcades, the city had laid down passerelle, narrow raised walkways of metal and wood, and the visitors, all twenty of them, shuffled along in single file like penitents on a pilgrimage, apologising to each other every time they collided.

There is now, to be fair, a technological defence. The enormous mobile barrier known as MOSE, a series of hinged steel gates on the sea floor at the entrances to the lagoon, was brought into operation in 2020, and it can be raised when a dangerous tide is forecast, sealing the lagoon from the Adriatic. It has been used dozens of times and has, on the whole, worked. Venetians regard it with the wary gratitude of people who have been rescued by a relative they do not entirely like. It is expensive, it is subject to long arguments, and it will, in time, need to be raised more and more often as the sea climbs. The grander question, whether a city can be saved forever by a gate, is one that Venice politely declines to answer.

By the afternoon the water had subsided, and the city, relieved, emptied its pockets into the cafés. I took refuge in a bacaro, one of those narrow wine bars where the clientele stands elbow to elbow, and ordered an ombra, a small glass of wine whose name means "shadow", a reference, it is said, to the days when vendors moved their stalls around the bell tower to keep their barrels out of the sun. With it came cicchetti: little squares of toasted bread piled with salt cod whipped into a cream, or sardines in a sour-sweet marinade of onions, raisins and pine nuts, the sort of food that tastes like an argument between sailors and merchants, settled in the sailors' favour.

An elderly man next to me, in a tweed cap that had seen several wars, asked where I was from, and on hearing the answer, nodded gravely. "You have come to see Venice sink," he said. "Everyone does. They are like the people who go to a hospital to look at the dying."

"I came to see it float," I said.

He considered this for a long moment, drained his glass, and conceded the point with a small, magnanimous bow. "Then you are the first of the year."

I spent the next three days on foot, which is the only honest way to know the city, for it is a labyrinth designed, apparently, by a committee of mischievous spiders. Streets end at canals without warning, bridges appear where there is no street, and the signs that read "Per San Marco" point with a confident vagueness in every direction at once. I was lost most of the time, and happily. Every wrong turning delivered me to some unexpected pleasure: a shuttered chapel with a Tintoretto in it, a boatyard where a man was bending oak for a gondola with the concentration of a violinist, a courtyard in which a single cat presided over a well.

On my last evening I stood on the Zattere, the long quay that faces the Giudecca, and watched the lights come on across the water, each doubled in the dark lagoon. A ferry droned past, a church bell conferred with another across the roofs, and the whole city seemed to breathe in, a slow and slightly damp inhalation. I understood then why people love it with such irrational stubbornness. Venice is not a place that conquers the sea but one that has agreed, after a thousand years of negotiation, to share its house with it. It is imperfect, endangered, and often wet, and it remains the loveliest argument ever made for the proposition that beauty and prudence do not need to be on speaking terms.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: MEL-an-chol-y, cer-e-MO-ni-al, mag-NAN-i-mous. Не ставьте ударение на последний слог по-русски.
Долгий, губы округлены, язык оттянут назад; не заменяйте на русское о или а.
Губы округлены и вытянуты вперёд, зубы нижнюю губу не касаются. Это не в.

questions.question: What is acqua alta?
questions.answer: High water: the flooding of Venice at high tide.

questions.question: What is MOSE?
questions.answer: A mobile barrier of steel gates protecting the lagoon.

questions.question: What is an ombra?
questions.answer: A small glass of wine, whose name means shadow.

questions.question: Why does the writer say he came to Venice?
questions.answer: To see it float rather than sink.
